Other piles
Deep foundation
A load-transferring element between the structure and the deeper bearing stratum that transfers load at its base and along its shaft. Types: pile, diaphragm wall, well and box foundations.
Tip resistance (base resistance)
The load transferred at the base of the pile by compression, like a shallow foundation.
Shaft (skin) resistance
The load transferred along the side surface of the pile by shear. In a tension pile only this works.
At least 2/3 of the resistance comes from the tip resistance: the pile “stands” in a much better layer.
At least 2/3 of the resistance comes from the shaft resistance; there is no layer of better bearing capacity near the tip.
The tip and the shaft resistance each contribute between 33 and 66 % of the resistance.
It transfers load only along its shaft, in the opposite direction – for example when anchoring against uplift or with a large eccentricity.
Pile grillage, pile cap
The reinforced concrete block, slab and/or grillage tying the pile heads together, which distributes the load of the superstructure onto the piles.
The soil is removed (bored out) and the hole is filled with concrete. Always cast in place; the surrounding soil may loosen slightly.
A precast element is driven, vibrated, jacked or screwed into the ground, or the soil is pushed aside in place – the surroundings are compacted.
Large-diameter pile
A pile with a diameter greater than 80 cm; made exclusively with replacement technology.
Pile driving
Installing a precast pile into the ground with a hammer (mechanical, pneumatic, steam or diesel hammer). Noisy, causes vibration; cannot be used in rock or hard clay.
By tuning the frequency to the natural frequency of the soil, the soil resistance temporarily drops to a minimum – mainly in granular soil.
A cased, cast-in-place driven concrete pile: the dry concrete plug placed in the tube is rammed with a drop hammer, and a “bulb” forms at the base.
A pile drilled with a continuous auger: the concrete is placed in the bore through the drill stem under excess pressure; 40–120 cm, 6–22 (24) m.
Soil plug
The soil remaining on the CFA auger, which supports the wall of the bore during drilling.
Necking
A local narrowing of the pile shaft, for example if the CFA drill stem is withdrawn faster than the concreting rate.
Casing (temporary casing)
A steel tube installed in parallel with soil removal, which prevents soil and water from breaking in until concreting.
Bentonite slurry (drilling mud)
Water with bentonite (montmorillonite) dispersed in it; it displaces the groundwater and supports the wall of the bore or trench. ρ = 1.03–1.12 g/cm³.
A concreting pipe whose end stays in the fresh concrete throughout: it concretes from the bottom up and displaces the slurry or water.
A cylindrical drilling tool for removing soil, mainly in granular soil.
A foundation excavated without support in cohesive soil above the groundwater, at most 5–6 m deep; also called a well foundation in Hungarian practice.
A pile with a diameter of at most 300 mm when bored, at most 150 mm when driven; for underpinning, in places with difficult access. No base resistance is assumed.
A wall in the ground built by reinforcing and concreting a vertical-sided trench supported by bentonite slurry; 40–120 cm thick.
Panel (primary, secondary)
The wall section excavated and concreted at once (typically 2.8–5.6 m). First the primary panels are made, then the secondary panels between them.
Bite
One excavation cycle of the grab; its length is typically 2.8 m, the open width of the grab.
A reinforced concrete beam built on both sides of the trench: it protects the edge, guides the tool and the slurry, and is the reference base for setting out.
The element marking the boundary between panels; it makes room for the swelling waterstop and protects the finished panel during the next excavation.
Silo effect
In a trench of finite length arching develops towards the two ends, so the earth pressure tends to a limit with depth (Schneebeli formula).
A reverse-circulation trenching machine with cutter wheels: it gives an accurate trench to great depth even in rock and very hard clay.
A large-diameter (0.8–3.0 m), 4–8 m long shell wall, open at the top and bottom, sunk by its own weight while the soil inside is removed.
Cutting edge
The reinforced lower edge of the sunk shell wall that cuts into the soil.
Box foundation
A sunk box matching the full plan of the structure (e.g. a bridge pier); it is built and sunk in stages.
A box closed at the top (“bell”), from which the water was expelled by an excess air pressure of at most 3.2–3.5 bar.
Airlock
A pressure-equalising chamber of the caisson: there is a separate airlock for people (with slow pressure change) and for materials.
Subsidence crater
A surface depression forming around the sunk box if the surrounding soil loosens.
